To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the structured clinical and epidemiologic assessment of temporally linked drug and medical event pairs can identify potential safety signals, but the false positive rate is unacceptably high without additional statistical analysis.

the structured assessment process we developed for the evaluation of drug–event combinations in electronic medical records can help to identify potential signals that merit further evaluation, but also to dismiss combinations that are not likely to represent new ADRs.

a process for structured assessment of temporally-associated drugs and medical events can be used to detect potential safety signals, but that effective signal detection requires combining statistical signal detection with clinical and epidemiology review to achieve an acceptably low false positive rate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of a process for structured, clinical, and epidemiological assessment in a longitudinal health database.
the evaluation of an exploratory approach that can be used to generate hypotheses for further evaluation, rather than for definitive conclusions.
the development and validation of a methodology to detect signals from electronic health data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the process described here is useful in detecting potential safety signals but that further research is needed to establish the most effective way to integrate the results from statistical analysis of longitudinal health data with clinical and epidemiologic review.
a potential ADR is not a signal unless the temporal pattern is suggestive and there is no plausible alternative explanation.

a signal is detected if the statistical signal detection method is combined with clinical and/or epidemiological review, and that a signal is not detected if the statistical method is not combined with clinical and/epidemiological review.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the process of structured assessment of temporally related drugs and medical events, as applied here, is feasible.
the process we developed is a useful addition to the signal detection toolbox.
the process of structured clinical and epidemiologic assessment of temporally-associated drugs and medical events can identify potential signals that merit further investigation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

signal detection in EMRs is feasible, but requires the development of a process that integrates the use of statistical methods and clinical/epidemiological judgment to achieve an acceptable signal detection rate.

a combination of epidemiological methods and clinical assessment of temporally related drug and medical event pairs in large electronic medical record databases is an efficient way to identify new safety signals for further investigation.
it is possible for a team of trained assessors to evaluate large numbers of drug–event combinations and to classify them according to their signal potential in a structured and efficient manner.
